Sometimes it matters that it was YOU. Not someone else. You yourself. Gupapuyŋu has a whole toolkit for this, emphasis, self, and own.

1. The emphatic -pi:
Add -pi to a pronoun and it becomes I myself / you yourself / he himself:
Ŋarrapi dhu marrtji → I myself will go (me, personally, not sending anyone)

2. The self-objects:
When the self is on the receiving end, the object pronouns from Lesson 11 grow a -pinya:
ŋarrapinya → myself
nhunapinya → yourself
ŋanyapinya → himself / herself

Ŋayi ŋanyapinya ḻupmaraŋala → He washed himself

3. The reflexive verb, Group 9:
And here's the elegant part. You often don't need a self-word at all, because the VERB itself can turn reflexive. Take the quaternary form and add -mi, and the action folds back onto its doer:

nhäma (to see) → nhänhamirri (to see oneself)
Ŋarra nhänhamina → I saw myself
Ŋayi ga nhänhamirri → She is looking at herself

If you've studied Hebrew, this is hitpa'el, a whole verb pattern whose only job is to reflect action back on the doer. Spanish does it with se, Ukrainian with -ся glued onto the verb. Same instinct, different tools: the mirror gets built into the verb.

And these reflexive verbs also carry the meaning of each other when the subject is plural. Two people seeing themselves... or seeing each other. Context decides, and honestly, in most real moments, the ambiguity is the point. The action stays inside the group.

4. Own, -wuy on the possessive:
One more: add -wuy (hello again, Lesson 18) to a possessive pronoun and my becomes my OWN:
Ŋarra waṯu bumara ŋarrakuwuy → I hit my own dog

Ŋarraku = my. Ŋarrakuwuy = my own, mine specifically, nobody else's.

Notice what all four tools share: they don't shout. English italicises, stresses, adds really and actually. Gupapuyŋu just places a small, precise suffix and lets it sit there. The emphasis is structural, not theatrical. You mark that it was you yourself, and then you move on.

Quiet precision. That's the register this language loves.
